# The Same 88 Keys

Give ten people the same camera, the same model, the same presets, and you get ten different results. Not close ones. Wildly different ones.

That gap used to be explained by access. Whoever had the sharper lens, the faster machine, the harder-to-learn tool won the argument before it started. That excuse is gone now. The tools are identical for everyone, and the output still refuses to be.

The tool was never the differentiator.

It was the excuse — a convenient one, because it pointed away from the person holding the tool and toward the object in their hands. Take the object away, or hand everyone the same one, and the excuse collapses. What's left is judgment: the ability to tell a good sentence from a merely competent one, a real idea from a plausible one, before either has been written down.

That ability doesn't come installed.

It comes from years of noticing what works and admitting, often in private, when it doesn't. For a long time, technical skill hid this problem well. Learning to draw or write or code took years, so the years of noticing happened by accident, folded quietly into the years of practicing the craft. Now the first draft is free, generated in seconds by a machine that has no opinion about whether it's any good.

The years of noticing have to happen on purpose now, or they don't happen at all.

The cheap part of the work has moved. Writing, drawing, building — a model does the mechanical part before you finish your coffee. What's expensive is knowing which of the hundred outputs is worth keeping, and most people were trained their whole lives to execute rather than to judge. That training doesn't transfer on its own, no matter how good the new tool is.

This is uncomfortable in a specific way. A tool that produces competent work by default doesn't hide a lack of taste. It exposes it, cleanly, with no technical struggle left to blame for the gap. The piano was always the same 88 keys, sitting there waiting for anyone to sit down. Some people played Bach, and most people played nothing worth naming, and the keys were never why.
